passages.t: ‘The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world’
passages.happening:
The tone of the letter changes. Paul begins gently, but with a sharp edge. “Now by the mildness and gentleness of Christ, I appeal to you” (verse 1). Then he names himself as his critics saw him: “I, Paul, who am humble when face to face with you, but bold when away” (verse 1).

He hopes he will not have to be bold when he comes, toward “those who presume that we live according to the flesh” (verse 2).

Then he explains how he fights. “For though we live in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world. Instead, they have divine power to demolish strongholds” (verses 3 and 4).

What strongholds? “We tear down arguments and every presumption set up against the knowledge of God; and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ” (verse 5).

He will be ready to deal with disobedience once the church as a whole has come back to obedience (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
From chapter 10 to the end, Paul speaks in a sharper, more hurt and more ironic voice. Some readers think chapters 10 to 13 were once a separate letter; others think Paul turns here to the rival teachers after first making peace with the church. The book page's part ‘One letter or several?’ sets out both views.

‘According to the flesh’ here means by merely human standards. Paul's critics said he lacked the things that made a leader impressive in Corinth.

Corinth was a Roman colony, and Rome's armies were famous for siege warfare. An army broke down a city's walls and towers and led its people away as prisoners. Paul uses that picture. But look at what he attacks. The ‘strongholds’ are ‘arguments’ and every proud claim ‘set up against the knowledge of God’. The prisoners are ‘thoughts’. His war is against ideas that keep people from God, not against people.

‘Take captive’ is, word for word, ‘capture with a spear’. Paul pictures a thought that has been fighting against Christ being brought over to his side. In context these are the claims of the rival teachers, who measured ministry by status and show. Paul means to answer them with the truth about Christ.

‘Gentleness’ in verse 1 is the Greek epieikeia: a readiness to yield rather than insist on one's rights. Paul opens his hardest chapters by naming the gentleness of Christ.
passages.ot:
Jesus described himself in the same words: “I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29).

The Old Testament speaks of pulling down proud strongholds by wisdom, not force. “A wise man scales the city of the mighty and pulls down the stronghold in which they trust” (Proverbs 21:22). Some readers hear that proverb behind Paul's picture.

It also knows that God's battles are not won by the world's weapons. Zechariah was told, “Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts” (Zechariah 4:6). David told the giant, “You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD of Hosts” (1 Samuel 17:45).

And God's word itself is pictured as a hammer that breaks rock. The LORD asks whether his word is not “like a hammer that smashes a rock” (Jeremiah 23:29).
passages.hard:
What are ‘the weapons of our warfare’, and what does ‘take captive every thought’ mean?

First, what they are not. Paul's war is not against people. His weapons have no force, no threats, no shouting down. Nothing here permits a Christian to be harsh or aggressive toward others, or to treat people who disagree as enemies to be beaten. Paul says in another letter, “our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (Ephesians 6:12). Some today speak of ‘spiritual warfare’ and aim it at a person: a neighbour, a family member, a political opponent. That is not what Paul is doing. He aims at false arguments, and even there his weapon is the truth about Christ, spoken with Christ's gentleness.

Second, ‘take captive every thought’ is about Paul's dealing with rival teaching in Corinth. He means bringing the church's thinking back under Christ. It is not a technique for pushing unwanted thoughts out of your mind.

Some people are troubled by unwanted thoughts that come again and again, often about the very things they most fear or hate. If that is you, hear this gently. Having such a thought is not the same as choosing it, and it is not sin. Trying harder to ‘capture’ it often makes it louder. This can be part of anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder, and it can be treated. A doctor or a counsellor can help, and a pastor or a friend you trust can stand with you. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul fights ideas with truth, not people with force. Ask whether you have ever treated a person as the enemy when the real problem was an idea. Then ask which of your own thoughts about God, yourself or others most need to be brought under Christ, gently and honestly.

passages.happening:
Paul tells the church to look past appearances. “You are looking at outward appearances. If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, he should remind himself that we belong to Christ just as much as he does” (verse 7).

He might boast a little too much about his authority, he says, but it is real, and it was given “for building you up rather than tearing you down” (verse 8). He does not want to frighten them with letters (verse 9).

He quotes what some are saying: “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account” (verse 10).

His answer is short. “Such people should consider that what we are in our letters when absent, we will be in our actions when present” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
In Greek cities, public speaking was an art and a show. Trained speakers were judged on their voice, their looks and their delivery as much as on what they said. Some became famous. To say a man's ‘physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account’ was a real insult in Corinth.

We do not know exactly what Paul looked like or how he spoke. The letter does not say. What it shows is that some in Corinth judged him by the standards of the stage.

‘Building you up rather than tearing you down’ is a key to Paul's authority. He says it again at the very end (13:10). Authority in the church is given to build people up. When it is used to tear them down, it has left its purpose.

The critics thought Paul was two people: brave on paper, weak in the room. Paul says he is one. If he must be firm when he comes, he will be.
passages.ot:
‘Building up, not tearing down’ comes from God's call to Jeremiah. “I have appointed you today over nations and kingdoms to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant” (Jeremiah 1:10). Jeremiah's word had both, and its last purpose was to build.

The warning against judging by appearance goes back to the choosing of David: “the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

And Moses himself, Israel's great leader, said he was a poor speaker: “I have never been eloquent” (Exodus 4:10). God used him anyway.
passages.asks: The Corinthians judged Paul by how he looked and spoke. Ask what you notice first about a speaker or a leader, and whether it is what matters most. Then ask whether the authority you have, at home, at work or in church, builds people up or tears them down.

passages.t: ‘Let him who boasts boast in the Lord’
passages.happening:
Paul will not join the comparison game. “When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they show their ignorance” (verse 12).

He will boast only within the limits God gave him, “a field that reaches even to you” (verse 13). He was the first to bring the gospel to Corinth (verse 14). He is not taking credit for other people's work (verse 15).

His hope is that as their faith grows, he can go further, “so that we can preach the gospel in the regions beyond you” (verse 16).

Then he gives the rule for all boasting: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (verse 17). “For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Listen to the repeated ‘themselves’ in verse 12. Paul is mocking gently. The rival teachers held up a ruler that they had made, and found that they measured well against it.

‘Limits’ and ‘field’ translate the Greek word kanōn. It meant a measuring rod, then a rule, then an area that had been measured out. Paul's point is that God had given him Corinth as part of his work. He founded the church there (Acts 18). The newcomers came into a church someone else had planted and claimed it as their own success.

‘The regions beyond you’ were the lands further west. A little later Paul wrote from Corinth to Rome, “I hope to see you on my way to Spain” (Romans 15:24).

In a city that loved self-praise, Paul's rule is simple. Your own praise of yourself proves nothing. The only praise that counts is the Lord's.
passages.ot:
Verse 17 sums up Jeremiah 9. The LORD says, “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the wealthy man in his riches” (Jeremiah 9:23). Instead, “let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am the LORD” (Jeremiah 9:24). Paul gives the heart of it in a few words, as he did in his first letter (1 Corinthians 1:31).

Jeremiah's list matches Corinth closely. Wisdom, strength and riches were what the city prized, and what the rivals claimed.

Proverbs adds the same warning about self-praise: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth” (Proverbs 27:2). And Hannah sang, “Do not boast so proudly, or let arrogance come from your mouth, for the LORD is a God who knows, and by Him actions are weighed” (1 Samuel 2:3).
passages.asks: Paul refused to measure himself against others. Ask whom you compare yourself with, and what it does to you. Then ask what it would mean to boast only in the Lord: to be glad in what he has done, and to wait for his ‘well done’ rather than other people's.
